notes: Stored edit with two background-belief queries (scouting 0002, fixed per the review). Derivability very_unlikely: the fact is stated everywhere and follows from nothing held more firmly. The scouting's 'can scurvy be treated with vitamin C?' query was dropped as near-definitional (a deficiency disease is treated by the missing nutrient, so its by-name world was close to inconsistent). It is replaced by the gums query: a symptom set that nutrition text ties to vitamin C directly as well as through scurvy, so a model may store it either way; both worlds are consistent, since a symptom can have several causes. Verifier: the writer's citrus query ('Does eating citrus fruit prevent scurvy?') was dropped. Its by-name world (citrus still prevents scurvy) contradicts firm facts outside the chain once scurvy is a vitamin D deficiency: citrus has no vitamin D, and a deficiency disease is prevented by supplying the missing nutrient. Step 3 drops that world, which leaves the query determinate (no), the same reason the scouting's 'vitamin C treats scurvy' query was dropped. It is replaced by a second sign of scurvy that text ties to vitamin C deficiency directly as well as through scurvy: corkscrew hairs and perifollicular bleeds (148 co-occurrences with 'vitamin C deficiency', 306 with 'scurvy'). Both by-name worlds are consistent, since a sign can have several causes; the two storage choices are likely correlated but are kept as independent (lopsided worlds kept, Decision 4). The two storage choices are independent, so four worlds. 'Ascorbic' and 'antiscorbutic' are kept out of every prompt (R2). R1: the gums prompt adds swollen gums and loose teeth because bleeding alone also follows vitamin K deficiency. Formal check (FINDINGS C2): q1's original 'no' rests on 'the skin does not make vitamin C', now a stated bridge with a check; the through-scurvy chains state the rule that ties a sign to the disease's missing nutrient.
